newsitem.title: CHINA: China lauds East Sea fleet after military exercise.
newsitem.headline: China lauds East Sea fleet after military exercise.

text.p: China on Monday hailed the power of its East Sea fleet, saying the nation's biggest war games at sea in more than 30 years demonstrated the nation's naval forces had achieved new levels of fighting power.

The fleet, which has the task of defending China's eastern seaboard and would be in the front line of any conflict with Japan or Taiwan, had held more than a week of competitive reviews of its combat ability, the China News Service said.
"From July 10 to July 20, the Liberation Army's East Sea fleet held the biggest contest in military techniques at sea since the all-forces contest of 1964," the agency said.

The exercise involved submarines, destroyers, escort vessels, landing craft and other vessels and tested sailors on more than 100 specialities, including the use of guided missiles, torpedoes, rockets and underwater guided weapons, it said.
"New records were set in tens of categories, indicating that the East Sea Fleet has raised its abilities in mastering modern weapons and equipment to a new level," it said.
The event was the latest in a series of training exercises and war games China has held in the East China Sea, one of its most sensitive strategic frontiers.

Military analysts have said the exercises are aimed at raising the effectiveness of China's army, navy and air force -- but also at reminding arch-rival Taiwan of the mainland's rapidly growing military clout.

Beijing considers Taiwan a rebel province and has warned it will invade the island if it ever declares formal independence, a threat that has been underlined in recent years by war games and guided missile tests in the Taiwan strait.

The East Sea fleet would also be a major factor in any military confrontation between Beijing and Tokyo, whose ties have long been strained by a territorial disagreement over a group of islands north of Taiwan.

A simmering dispute over the islands, known in China as the Diaoyus and in Japan as the Senkakus, flared over the past year after a series of landings on them by Japanese nationalists, but both governments have been keen to put the dispute aside.

While military analysts say the technical level of China's navy lags far behind those of Taiwan, Japan or Western nations, few doubt Beijing's determination to turn its fleets into a credible regional force.

Modernisation backed by Admiral Liu Huaqing, a member of the elite politburo and China's highest ranking military officer, has brought new destroyers, frigates and submarines, greatly boosting naval effectiveness in some areas, analysts have said.
The East Sea fleet had strengthened its training regime, enabling it to make full use of the fighting power brought by its new hardware, the China News Service said.

"In recent years, following the historic project of the modernisation of the Chinese People's Liberation Army, the main fighting vessels of the East Sea fleet have greatly raised their use of guided missiles, electronics and automation," it said.
